column2: Site ten needs five hundred and twenty pounds more a week to break even. Some of it may already be walking out of the door. Every lunchtime. In the queue.

John Little proved it in nineteen sixty-one. The number of people in a queue equals how fast they arrive, times how long they wait. Owners rarely use it. But turn it round, and two numbers you can count tell you the third.
Count your lunch queue at ten past twelve. Twelve people. Now count how fast the till serves. Two a minute. So the last person in that queue waits six minutes.

Six minutes is long enough for some guests to give up. Say ten a day walk away, at eight pounds fifty each. Over six days, that's five hundred and ten pounds a week. Almost exactly what site ten is missing.
The fix isn't more staff all day. It's the bottleneck at noon. Serve three a minute instead of two, and the same queue waits four minutes, not six.
Your question for Monday: at ten past twelve, how long is your lunch queue really waiting?
